cultures/culture-reformations/panels/0/t: Protestants worshipped in the vernacular with preaching at the centre; Lutherans kept much of the Mass, Reformed churches stripped worship to Scripture-commanded elements, Anglicans used the Book of Common Prayer. Catholics standardised the Roman Missal (1570), and missions adapted liturgy in Nahuatl, Tamil and Japanese.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/1/t: Luther's chorales ('A Mighty Fortress') and the Genevan Psalter put song in congregations' mouths. Palestrina exemplified Counter-Reformation polyphony; Indigenous choirs in New Spain sang European polyphony within decades of conquest.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/2/t: Il Gesù in Rome and the completion of St Peter's set the Baroque model of open naves for preaching and spectacle, copied in Goa and Mexico. Reformed churches whitewashed images and arranged seating around the pulpit.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/3/t: Reformed iconoclasm destroyed images in Switzerland, Scotland and the Netherlands, while Lutherans kept altarpieces (Cranach). Catholic art emphasised saints, sacraments and ecstasy; Indigenous artists created Mexican feather mosaics and Japanese Christian 'Namban' art.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/4/t: Protestant territories dissolved monasteries and convents. Catholic renewal produced Jesuits, Capuchins, Ursulines, Discalced Carmelites and Oratorians; Orthodox monasticism endured under Ottoman rule.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/5/t: Reformed calendars and the Gregorian calendar

Protestants pruned saints' days, Puritans abolished Christmas; Catholics retained the full calendar. Gregory XIII's calendar reform (1582) was adopted by Catholic states immediately but by Protestants later and never for Orthodox church festivals.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/6/t: Katharina von Bora modelled the Protestant pastor's household, and Argula von Grumbach wrote in defence of reform. Teresa of Ávila reformed the Carmelites; Anabaptist women died as martyrs; Japanese women catechists sustained Christian communities.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/7/t: Catechisms (Luther, Heidelberg, Canisius, Roman) taught every confession. Jesuit colleges, Calvin's Academy and Protestant universities trained clergy; the first printing presses in Mexico (1539), Goa (1556) and Japan (1590) served missions.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/8/t: Franciscans, Dominicans and Jesuits evangelised the Americas, the Philippines, Japan, China, India and Kongo, with debates over accommodation. Protestant missions barely began, though John Eliot evangelised Algonquians in New England.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/9/t: Catholics, Protestants and Anabaptists were executed by rival regimes — Foxe's Book of Martyrs and Catholic martyrologies told competing stories. Japan's persecution after 1614 killed thousands; St Bartholomew's Day and the Thirty Years' War brought mass violence.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/10/: Luther moved from hope of Jewish conversion to violent polemic (1543). Paul IV confined Rome's Jews to a ghetto (1555), while Poland-Lithuania and the Netherlands offered relative refuge.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/11/: Ottoman advances to Vienna (1529) shaped German politics, and Luther saw the Turk as God's scourge. Ethiopia nearly fell to Ahmad Gragn of Adal (1529–43) until Portuguese aid arrived; Lepanto (1571) became a Catholic symbol.
cultures/culture-reformations/panels/12/: Princes and cities determined their territory's religion; England's monarch became supreme governor of the church; Anabaptists alone rejected the sword. Spain and Portugal controlled overseas churches through patronato, and Westphalia (1648) fixed confessional borders.
cultures/culture-confessional-pietism/pa: Orthodoxy and heart religion

Lutheran and Reformed orthodoxy produced long doctrinal sermons, while Pietist conventicles met for Bible study and prayer. Quakers waited in silence for the Spirit. In Russia, Nikon's liturgical reforms divided the church; in Kerala, Thomas Christians reasserted Syriac liturgy.
Bach and Isaac Watts
Lutheran church music reached its summit with Buxtehude and J. S. Bach's cantatas and Passions. Isaac Watts' hymns (1707) broke the dominance of metrical psalms in English-speaking churches.
Meeting houses and Baroque

Dissenters and New England Congregationalists built plain meeting houses with central pulpits; Wren rebuilt London's churches after 1666 as auditory spaces. Catholic Baroque flourished in Austria and Latin America, and Russian 'Naryshkin Baroque' blended Western ornament with Orthodox forms.
Plainness and splendour

Protestant devotion favoured printed emblems, portraits and the Bible over altars, while Catholic Baroque art (Bernini, Murillo) celebrated saints and the Virgin. Cusco and Quito schools of painting produced Andean Christian art.
Port-Royal and the Old Believers

The Jansenist convent of Port-Royal became a centre of Augustinian piety until its suppression (1709). Old Believers formed hermit communities in Russian forests, and Moravian 'choirs' at Herrnhut organised life by age and sex in a quasi-monastic way.
Days of humiliation and thanksgiving

Puritans replaced saints' days with Sabbath observance and special days of fasting and thanksgiving. Catholic Europe added feasts like the Sacred Heart devotion following Margaret Mary Alacoque's visions (1670s).
Quaker preachers and Kimpa Vita

Quakers accepted women as preachers, like Margaret Fell, who defended it in Women's Speaking Justified (1666). Madame Guyon taught quietist prayer; in Kongo Kimpa Vita led a prophetic movement. Pietist women ran conventicles and wrote spiritual autobiographies.
Halle and Jesuit science

August Hermann Francke's Halle foundations (1695) combined orphanage, schools, press and mission training. Jesuit astronomers served the Qing court, and the Tranquebar mission founded schools and a Tamil press.
Pietist and Jesuit missions

The Danish-Halle mission began Protestant work in India (1706); Moravians would soon follow. Jesuit reductions in Paraguay organised Guaraní towns, and Capuchins worked in Kongo, while the Chinese Rites controversy limited Catholic growth in China.
Huguenots, Old Believers and Covenanters

France revoked toleration (1685) and persecuted Huguenots; Russia persecuted Old Believers; Scottish Covenanters were killed in the 'Killing Time'. English Dissenters faced fines and prison until 1689.
Philo-Semitism and millennial hopes

Cromwell's England readmitted Jews (1656), encouraged by millennial hopes of Jewish conversion. The Sabbatai Zevi movement (1665–66) electrified Jewish communities; Halle Pietists founded a mission to Jews (1728).
Vienna 1683 and Ottoman Christians

The Ottoman siege of Vienna failed (1683), beginning a long retreat in Europe. Orthodox, Armenian and other Christians in the Ottoman Empire lived as millets, and Catholic missions created Eastern Catholic communities in the Levant, such as the Melkite Catholics (1724).
Toleration and state churches

England's Act of Toleration (1689), Locke's Letter on Toleration and Rhode Island and Pennsylvania's religious liberty pointed toward freedom of conscience. Peter the Great subordinated the Russian church to a state synod (1721), and absolutist France enforced Catholic uniformity.
cultures/culture-awakenings-missions/pan: Field preaching and camp meetings

Evangelical revival moved worship outdoors: Whitefield and Wesley preached to thousands in fields; American camp meetings lasted days with shouting and falling. Methodist class meetings and love feasts fostered testimony, and African American worship developed its own call-and-response traditions.
Hymns of experience and spirituals

Charles Wesley's and John Newton's hymns ('Amazing Grace', 1779) taught evangelical experience; Russian and Orthodox churches developed choral styles (Bortniansky). Enslaved African Americans created spirituals that blended biblical narrative with African musical forms.
Chapels and preaching houses

Methodists built plain preaching houses and chapels; Nonconformist chapels filled industrial towns. Missionaries erected churches across the Pacific and Africa often in local materials, while Gothic Revival began to return in the 1840s.
Prints and Romanticism
Cheap prints, tracts and illustrated Bibles spread evangelical imagery. Romantic and Nazarene painters revived medieval religious art; in Russia, popular icons and lubok prints expressed folk piety.
Suppression and revival

The French Revolution dissolved monasteries, Joseph II closed contemplative houses in Austria, and the Jesuits were suppressed (1773–1814). Orthodoxy saw a revival of eldership: Paisius Velichkovsky, Seraphim of Sarov and the startsy of Optina.
Revolutionary calendars and Sabbath reform

Revolutionary France abolished the Christian calendar (1793–1805), while evangelicals campaigned for strict Sunday observance. Missionary prayer meetings and anniversaries became new rhythms in Protestant life.
Societies, sisters and preachers

Women ran Sunday schools, missionary auxiliaries and abolition campaigns; some, such as early Methodist and AME preacher Jarena Lee, preached. Catholic active orders of sisters multiplied in nursing and teaching.
Sunday schools and colleges

Robert Raikes' Sunday schools (1780) taught poor children to read; American revivals founded colleges and seminaries. Serampore College (1818) and Fourah Bay College (1827) were early Christian higher education institutions in Asia and Africa.
The great century begins

Voluntary societies (BMS 1792, LMS 1795, CMS 1799, ABCFM 1810) sent missionaries to India, the Pacific, Africa and China. Islander and African evangelists often carried the faith further than Europeans; Korean laymen founded their own Catholic church.
Revolution, Korea and Madagascar

The French Revolution's dechristianisation killed priests and nuns. Korean Catholics suffered waves of martyrdom (1801, 1839, 1846); Queen Ranavalona persecuted Malagasy Christians; Vietnamese Catholics were executed under Minh Mạng.
Emancipation and mission

Jewish civil emancipation began in revolutionary France (1791) and spread across Western Europe. The London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews (1809) reflected evangelical eschatological hopes.
Colonialism and Eastern Christians

Napoleon's invasion of Egypt (1798) opened the Middle East to Western missions, which mostly converted Eastern Christians rather than Muslims. In West Africa the Sokoto jihad (1804) expanded Islam just as Christian missions began; Henry Martyn translated the New Testament into Persian and Urdu.
Disestablishment and religious freedom

The US First Amendment (1791) barred a federal established church, and states disestablished by 1833. Napoleon's Concordat (1801) restored Catholicism in France under state control; newly independent Latin American states wrestled with the church's patronage and privileges.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/0/tex: Anglo-Catholics restored vestments and Eucharistic devotion; the Catholic liturgical movement began; revivalists like Moody used gospel songs and altar calls. Pentecostal worship after 1906 featured tongues, healing and spontaneous praise, and African independent churches incorporated drumming, dance and white robes.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/1/tex: Fanny Crosby's and Ira Sankey's gospel songs spread worldwide, Black gospel music emerged in the 1930s (Thomas Dorsey), and Pentecostals adopted popular instruments. Rachmaninoff's All-Night Vigil (1915) and Solesmes' restoration of Gregorian chant revived older traditions.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/2/tex: Gothic Revival churches and cathedrals were built from London to Lagos, Mumbai and Sydney. Evangelical congregations built 'auditorium' churches like Spurgeon's Metropolitan Tabernacle and Akron-plan buildings with sloping floors and choir lofts.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/3/tex: Mass-produced religious images (Sacred Heart, Warner Sallman's Head of Christ, 1940) filled homes. Some modern artists (Rouault) treated Christian themes, while African and Asian Christian artists began to depict Christ in local forms.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/4/tex: Anglican religious orders revived after 1841; Catholic missionary orders like the White Fathers (1868) and Mill Hill multiplied; Benedictine renewal flourished at Solesmes and Beuron. Orthodox monasticism suffered under Soviet rule after 1917.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/5/tex: Catholics added Christ the King (1925); many Orthodox churches adopted the Revised Julian calendar (1923) for fixed feasts, provoking Old Calendarist schisms. Missionary churches debated Christianising local festivals.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/6/tex: By 1900 women formed the majority of Protestant missionaries; Bible women in China and India evangelised homes; Pandita Ramabai founded Mukti. Holiness and Pentecostal churches ordained women (Aimee Semple McPherson), and the Salvation Army gave women equal rank.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/7/tex: Mission schools educated many leaders of independent Africa and Asia; Christian universities were founded in China, Korea, Japan and India. Historical criticism reshaped Protestant seminaries, prompting the fundamentalist reaction; Catholic modernism was condemned (1907).
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/8/tex: Under colonial expansion, missions reached the African interior and inland China; African prophets (Harris, Kimbangu, Shembe) and Asian revivals indigenised Christianity. Edinburgh 1910 launched the ecumenical movement; Pentecostal missionaries spread worldwide after Azusa Street.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/9/tex: The Armenian genocide and Sayfo (1915), Soviet persecution after 1917, the Boxer Uprising (1900), Mexico's Cristero War and the Spanish Civil War killed many Christians. In Nazi Germany Confessing Church pastors were imprisoned; Bonhoeffer was executed in 1945.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/10/te: Christian anti-Judaism fed modern racial antisemitism; pogroms in the Russian Empire were often justified religiously. During the Holocaust most churches failed to resist, though some Christians rescued Jews (Le Chambon, the 'righteous among the nations'). This failure later prompted profound repentance.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/11/te: Christian missions and Islamic expansion competed in Africa; colonial powers often limited missions in Muslim areas. Missionaries like Samuel Zwemer focused on Muslims with little numerical success, while Middle Eastern Christians helped lead the Arab cultural renaissance.
cultures/culture-modern-era/panels/12/te: France separated church and state (1905); the papacy lost its states (1870) and gained Vatican City (1929). Soviet, Nazi and fascist states persecuted or co-opted churches; Japanese authorities required shrine attendance in Korea. Churches also supported nationalist movements in Ireland, Poland and Africa.
